sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in downtown Cincinnati
National Register of Historic Places listings in Cincinnati
Wikipedia GeoSearch, 3 km radius around Fountain Square

stops.name: Tyler Davidson Fountain
stops.description: The Genius of Water has poured rain from her outstretched fingers over this square since 1871, cast in Munich and shipped across in sections for assembly.

stops.name: Carew Tower
stops.description: Cincinnati's tallest building from 1930 until 2011, and a National Historic Landmark the Park Service calls one of the finest examples of skyscraper modernism in America.

stops.name: Ingalls Building
stops.description: The world's first reinforced concrete skyscraper, finished in 1903, with a reporter reputedly waiting up all night to be first to report it falling down.

stops.name: Dixie Terminal
stops.description: Streetcars off the Roebling bridge once rolled straight into this 1921 terminal, and its Rookwood tile entry arch is still above the door.

stops.name: Contemporary Arts Center
stops.description: Zaha Hadid's first American building, housing the museum acquitted in 1990 in the first criminal obscenity trial of an art museum in the country.

stops.name: Christ Church Cathedral
stops.description: Founded in 1817 by a group that included the future president William Henry Harrison, and the 1957 building still carries stained glass salvaged from its 1835 predecessor.

stops.name: Taft Museum of Art
stops.description: William Howard Taft accepted his presidential nomination from the portico of this 1820 Federal house, now a museum built around Robert Duncanson's wall murals.

stops.name: Abraham Lincoln Statue, Lytle Park
stops.description: George Grey Barnard's eleven-foot bronze Lincoln was unveiled in this park in 1917, with William Howard Taft giving the dedication speech.

stops.name: National Underground Railroad Freedom Center
stops.description: Sited where thousands crossed the Ohio River out of slavery, and holding the only known surviving rural slave jail, moved here out of a Kentucky tobacco barn.

stops.name: John A. Roebling Suspension Bridge
stops.description: The longest suspension bridge in the world when it opened in 1867, by the engineer who went on to design the Brooklyn Bridge, and still open to walk across.

stops.name: Cincinnati City Hall
stops.description: Samuel Hannaford's 1893 Richardsonian Romanesque seat of government, where windows shrink as they climb so the facade reads taller than it stands.

stops.name: Isaac M. Wise Temple
stops.description: Built in 1866 for the rabbi who helped found American Reform Judaism, with a Moorish Revival interior drawn from the Alhambra.

stops.name: Cathedral Basilica of St. Peter in Chains
stops.description: A 224-foot spire made this 1845 Greek Revival cathedral the tallest thing in Cincinnati for decades, and Pope Francis named it a minor basilica in 2020.

stops.name: Piatt Park
stops.description: Cincinnati's oldest park, laid out in 1817, with a president at either end: Garfield toward Vine Street and Harrison on the only equestrian statue in the city.

stops.name: Arnold's Bar and Grill
stops.description: The oldest continuously operating bar in Cincinnati, pouring since 1861, with a second-floor bathtub said to have produced gin during Prohibition.

note: Cincinnati has never been scouted in the 12 runs on record, so it won outright. All 15 stops sit in the central business district between the riverfront and Garfield Place, roughly a 2 mile loop end to end rather than 1 mile, because the Taft Museum on the east side and City Hall on the west are both too good to drop. Two verified stops were held back deliberately as Over-the-Rhine outliers, 0.9 mi north of the core across Central Parkway, and they would anchor a future OTR run well: Cincinnati Music Hall (1241 Elm St, 45202, National Historic Landmark, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Music_Hall) and Hamilton County Memorial Building next door (1225 Elm St, 45202, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_County_Memorial_Building). Findlay Market was dropped as a genuine outlier at about 1.8 mi north. The Roebling Suspension Bridge is the one stop with a null address and null zip: it spans the Ohio River and has no street number, and per the rules a zip was not derived from its coordinates. Every other stop carries a verified 45202, the single zip covering the whole CBD. Addresses came from the downtown NRHP listing table and were cross-checked against each place's own article; where an article gave only a cross street (Fountain Square, Dixie Terminal, Lytle Park, Piatt Park) the street number was looked up independently rather than guessed. Note that the Contemporary Arts Center's NRHP row points at its former home at 120 E 4th St, not the current Zaha Hadid building at 44 E 6th St used here.
